paragraphs.text: Cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. According to Yoshida et al. (2015), its clinical manifestations comprise a unique facial appearance with cleft lip/palate, ectodermal dysplasia, cutaneous syndactyly of the fingers and/or toes, and in some cases, mental retardation. Suzuki et al. (1998) described the disorder as Margarita Island ectodermal dysplasia, characterized by unusual facies, dental anomalies, hypotrichosis, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and onychodysplasia, syndactyly, and cleft lip/cleft palate.

paragraphs.text: Bustos et al. (1991) described 27 individuals from 7 families, related to each other with high probability, from a relatively isolated and inbred population on Margarita Island in northeastern Venezuela (Nueva Esparta State). The patients showed manifestations of ectodermal dysplasia and other anomalies, with females affected as severely as males and with variable expressivity. All parents were normal. The authors considered the condition to be a newly recognized autosomal recessive dysplasia/malformation syndrome that could not be classified within the known ectodermal dysplasias.

paragraphs.text: Zlotogora et al. (1987) suggested autosomal recessive inheritance on the basis of affected sibs. Parental consanguinity was reported by Oğur and Yüksel (1988), Rodini and Richieri-Costa (1990), and Yoshida et al. (2015), and Bustos et al. (1991) considered the Margarita Island disorder, in which all parents were normal, to be autosomal recessive. Homozygous PVRL1 mutations in affected individuals (Sözen et al., 2001; Yoshida et al., 2015) confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance.

paragraphs.text: By positional cloning, Suzuki et al. (2000) identified PVRL1, encoding nectin-1, an immunoglobulin-related transmembrane cell-cell adhesion molecule, as the gene responsible for autosomal recessive CLPED1. Nectin-1 is also the principal cell surface receptor for alpha-herpesviruses, and the authors suggested that the high frequency of CLPED1 on Margarita Island might result from resistance of heterozygotes to infection by these viruses.

checks.evidence_quote: Here we demonstrate highly significant association between heterozygosity for this mutation and sporadic, non-syndromic CL/P in northern Venezuela.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

paragraphs.text: In a 7-year-old Japanese boy with CLPED1, the first child of a consanguineous marriage, Yoshida et al. (2015) identified a homozygous c.400C-T transition in exon 2 of the PVRL1 gene, resulting in an arg134-to-ter (R134X) substitution. His parents were heterozygous for the mutation. The predicted truncated protein lacks the transmembrane and intracellular domains of nectin-1.

checks.claim: Yoshida et al. (2015) identified a homozygous c.400C-T transition in exon 2 of the PVRL1 gene, resulting in an arg134-to-ter (R134X) substitution, in a 7-year-old Japanese boy with CLPED1.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutation analysis of exon 2 of PVRL1 revealed a novel homozygous nonsense mutation, c.400C>T (p.Arg134*).
checks.explanation: Same variant in equivalent notation; C>T is a transition.

checks.claim: The Japanese boy with CLPED1 homozygous for PVRL1 R134X reported by Yoshida et al. (2015) was the first child of a consanguineous marriage.
checks.evidence_quote: A 7-year-old Japanese boy, the first child of a consanguineous marriage
checks.explanation: The paper says he was the first child of a consanguineous marriage.

checks.claim: The parents of the Japanese boy with CLPED1 reported by Yoshida et al. (2015) were heterozygous for the PVRL1 R134X mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: His parents were heterozygous for the mutant alleles.
checks.explanation: The paper says both parents were heterozygous carriers.

checks.claim: The truncated nectin-1 protein predicted from the PVRL1 R134X mutation lacks the transmembrane and intracellular domains.
checks.evidence_quote: All four PVRL1 mutations identified in cleft lip/palate-ectodermal dysplasia syndrome to date, including this study, resulted in truncated proteins that lack the transmembrane domain and intracellular domain of nectin-1
checks.explanation: The paper's statement covers the R134X mutation from this study.

agent.process_note: I opened all 11 files. None has a full text: 8 are abstracts only and 3 are titles only (Rosselli and Gulienetti 1961, Zlotogora and Ogur 1988, Zlotogora 1994). I did not cite the title-only papers because they contain no facts. The Suzuki et al. (2000) abstract names PVRL1 but gives no mutation. W185X comes only from the Sözen et al. (2001) abstract, and no nucleotide change is given for it. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so the gene's MIM number is left out. The 11q23 location comes from the mapping by Suzuki et al. (1998).
